title: Drive a case interview by proposing your next step after every answer instead of waiting to be told
description: In candidate-led cases you are expected to steer, and even in interviewer-led ones, proposing next steps earns credit. Summarise as you go, and keep linking b
hook: Many candidates do well in the opening and then drift, waiting for the interviewer to tell them what to do next. Interviewers notice. Driving the case simply means that after every answer, you say what it means and where you want to go next. This guide shows you how to do that without sounding pushy.
body:
In this guide

  • Propose, don’t wait
  • Summarise at the turns
  • Link every finding to the goal
  • When you get lost
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Propose, don’t wait

After your structure, and after every answer, say what you want to look at next, what data you need, and why: "As a next step, I’d like to check whether the drop is industry-wide. Do we have market data?" This is what interviewers mean by case leadership, and it’s scored separately from getting the answers right.

Summarise at the turns

When you finish one branch of your structure, give a two-line summary before moving on: "So far: revenue is flat, and the profit drop is almost all delivery commissions. The open question is whether delivery adds any profit at all." It keeps the interviewer with you, and it keeps you oriented.

Link every finding to the goal

Finish each finding with why it matters for the client: "...which matters because our goal is to get back to $10M." If you can’t link a finding to the goal, it probably isn’t important.

When you get lost

It happens to everyone. Don’t go silent. Step back out loud: "Let me take a step back. We know A and B, and we’re trying to get to X, so the next thing to check is C." A calm step back reads as composure; panic reads as panic.

See it in action: After reading a chart

Passive: "So the North fell a lot. What would you like me to look at next?"

Driving: "The North explains the whole decline, while other regions grew slightly. Given our goal is to restore sales, I’d like to understand what changed in the North: did we lose a big customer, close stores, or face a new competitor? Do we have sales by customer for the North?"

What to remember

  • End every answer with your next step and the data you need.
  • Summarise when you finish a branch.
  • Link findings back to the goal; step back out loud when lost.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. You’ve just finished analysing costs. What should you do next?

  • Wait for the interviewer’s next question
  • Summarise what you found and propose the next area to look at
  • Start your recommendation immediately
Show the answer

Summarise what you found and propose the next area to look at. A quick summary plus a proposed next step is exactly what case leadership looks like.

2. You realise you’re lost mid-case. What’s the best move?

  • Keep talking until something comes to you
  • Pause and step back out loud: what we know, what we need, what to check next
  • Ask the interviewer for the answer
Show the answer

Pause and step back out loud: what we know, what we need, what to check next. Stepping back calmly shows composure and usually reveals the next step.

Try it now

You’ve just found that delivery-app commissions explain most of Coastal Brew’s profit fall. Say your next step out loud, in two sentences, the way you would to the interviewer.

Give yourself 45 seconds, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

"So the profit drop is mostly delivery commissions, which matters because they now eat 7.6% of revenue. Next, I’d like to compare the profit on a delivery order with an in-store order, to see whether delivery adds any profit at all. Do we have the economics per order?"
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 4 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
